But to take on the role of tabloid editor Larry Lamb, he got even more comfortable with suave, alluring menace.

“His prerogative is very simple,” O’Connell says over Zoom from London. “He’s fixated on sales numbers and whatever it’s going to take to keep that figure rising. He’ll stop at nothing — and that means bending the rules. It was very naughty.”

Netflix’s “Ink,” directed by Danny Boyle and set to open the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 2, is as naughty as its central character. Lamb was the real-life editor of The Sun who — hired in 1969 by press baron Rupert Murdoch to help the tabloid break into the U.K. newspaper industry — pioneered such practices as publishing nude pictures of “Page 3 Girls.” The provocative biopic, however, is not intended as a hit piece.

“One of the dangers with doing anything about Rupert Murdoch is that everybody monster-izes him,” says director Danny Boyle, “as though he’s forced everybody to read The Sun! We are all responsible for this.”

Her larger-than-life hair, excess in rhinestones, surgical implants, and cosmetic work concealed the iron will through which she confronted the day’s realities with her craft. She wrote and sang with a woman’s voice and heart about topics that touched her gender, like stories of stillborn births (“Down From Dover”), suicide (“The Bridge”), shame (“Just Because I’m a Woman”), sexual assault (“A Gamble Either Way”), isolation (“Two Doors Down”), and prostitution (“The Bargain Store”).
